notes.front: What does small UAS maintenance include, according to AC 107-2A?
notes.back: Scheduled and unscheduled overhaul, repair, inspection, modification, replacement, and system software upgrades of the small UAS and its components.
notes.explanation: Keeping every part in a condition for safe operation is what lets the remote PIC pass the check required before each flight.
notes.example: Replacing a chipped propeller, or installing a firmware update the manufacturer requires, are both maintenance.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2, p. 7-1

notes.front: What is scheduled maintenance for a small UAS?
notes.back: Periodic maintenance or replacement of components based on time-in-service limits, such as flight hours, cycles (e.g. number of flights) or calendar days.
notes.explanation: Following the manufacturer’s schedule gives the longest and safest service life.
notes.example: Replacing motors after the number of flight hours the manufacturer specifies.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.1, p. 7-1

notes.front: What is unscheduled maintenance for a small UAS?
notes.back: Servicing, repair, modification, overhaul or replacement needed outside the schedule, from normal use, a mishap, or a required software update.
notes.explanation: It is often found during a preflight inspection, and flight should not happen until the issue is fixed.
notes.example: Finding a cracked arm after a hard landing and replacing it before the next flight.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.2, p. 7-1

notes.front: What is the preflight inspection of a small UAS?
notes.back: A check of the whole system before each flight, for damage or malfunction, to confirm it is in a condition for safe operation.
notes.explanation: It is required before every flight and should follow the manufacturer’s procedure, the owner’s own procedure, or both.
notes.example: Walking round the aircraft checking props, arms, battery and camera mount, then testing the controls.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3, p. 7-2

notes.front: What is 14 CFR part 43 appendix D, in small UAS inspection?
notes.back: A manned-aircraft maintenance inspection checklist that some operators use as a guide to build their own inspection programme.
notes.explanation: It divides the aircraft into subgroups, giving a logical order, but it misses UAS-specific items.
notes.example: Inspecting the airframe, then the flight controls, then the batteries, then the engine, in turn.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.3, p. 7-2

notes.front: What is maintenance record keeping for a small UAS?
notes.back: Documenting every repair, modification, overhaul or replacement, with the component’s time-in-service at that moment.
notes.explanation: Records turn experience into a reliable maintenance schedule and show that the system is fit to launch.
notes.example: A logbook entry: “Rear-left motor replaced at 42 flight hours, 12 May.”
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.5, p. 7-4

notes.front: AC 107-2A counts not only repair and replacement as small UAS maintenance, but also {{c1::system software upgrades}}.
notes.explanation: A manufacturer may require an unscheduled software update to correct a problem.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2, p. 7-1

notes.front: Whenever possible, whose instructions should an operator follow when maintaining a small UAS?
notes.back: The manufacturer’s.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer may provide the maintenance programme; if not, the operator may develop one.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2, p. 7-1

notes.front: If no manufacturer provides scheduled maintenance instructions, what should the operator do?
notes.back: Establish their own protocol: record each repair or replacement and the component’s time-in-service, and build a schedule from that.
notes.explanation: Over time the records show how long components really last.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.1.1, p. 7-1

notes.front: On what can a manufacturer base time-in-service limits for components?
notes.back: Flight hours, cycles and/or calendar days.
notes.explanation: Cycles are counts of use, such as the number of flights. Components reaching those limits undergo scheduled maintenance or replacement.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.1, p. 7-1

notes.front: A preflight inspection finds a component needing repair outside the schedule. When may flight continue?
notes.back: Only after the issue is corrected.
notes.explanation: Unscheduled maintenance can result from normal use, a mishap or a required software update.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.2, p. 7-1

notes.front: Who may a manufacturer require to perform certain maintenance tasks?
notes.back: The manufacturer itself, or a person or facility it specifies.
notes.explanation: Maintenance should follow the manufacturer’s instructions.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.3, p. 7-1

notes.front: If the operator does not use the manufacturer or its recommended personnel, whom should they consider?
notes.back: Maintenance personnel with expertise in, and familiar with, that specific small UAS and its components.
notes.explanation: If they still cannot restore it to its safe specification, the component should be replaced.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.3, p. 7-2

notes.front: If a component cannot be repaired back to its safe operational specification, what should the operator do?
notes.back: Replace the small UAS or component with one in a condition for safe operation.
notes.explanation: All required maintenance should be finished before each flight.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.3.1, p. 7-2

notes.front: For a Category 4 small UA, what must the person doing maintenance have?
notes.back: The knowledge, skill and appropriate equipment to perform the work.
notes.explanation: They must also use the manufacturer’s current maintenance methods or others acceptable to the FAA.
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.140(c) “Category 4 operations” (maintenance requirements) (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: For a Category 4 aircraft, what must each maintenance record contain?
notes.back: A description of the work, the date it was completed, and the name of the person who did it.
notes.explanation: The owner (or operator by agreement) must keep these records.
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.140(c) “Category 4 operations” (maintenance requirements) (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: How often must the remote PIC check the small UA to determine it is in a condition for safe operation?
notes.back: Before each flight (§107.15).
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A chapter 7 gives the guidance for doing that check.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.1, p. 7-1

notes.front: Whose procedure should a preflight inspection follow?
notes.back: The manufacturer’s inspection procedure when available, and/or one developed by the owner or operator.
notes.explanation: Manufacturer procedures are usually in the owner’s or maintenance manual.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3, p. 7-2

notes.front: What should a scalable preflight inspection cover?
notes.back: The entire system, scaled to the small UAS, the programme and the operation.
notes.explanation: A check of the aircraft alone would miss the control station, links and support equipment.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.2, p. 7-2

notes.front: If the manufacturer already provides a written preflight procedure, does the FAA still recommend adding its own list of items?
notes.back: Yes; the FAA recommends including its listed items in the remote PIC’s preflight procedure anyway.
notes.explanation: That ensures the remote PIC accurately determines the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4, p. 7-2

notes.front: What general check of the aircraft’s parts opens the AC’s recommended preflight list?
notes.back: A visual condition inspection of the small UAS components.
notes.explanation: A look over every part comes first; the AC recommends its 23 checks even when the manufacturer has its own preflight procedure.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 1, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to check about the airframe?
notes.back: Its structure, including the undercarriage, all flight control surfaces and linkages.
notes.explanation: The airframe carries every other part; the AC’s condition chart lists signs such as cracks and delamination that call for further inspection.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 2, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to check about registration markings?
notes.back: That they are properly displayed and legible (§48.205).
notes.explanation: Part 48 (§ 48.205) requires the registration marking to be displayed and legible, so a scuffed or covered marking fails the rule.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 3, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to check about moveable control surfaces?
notes.back: The surfaces themselves and their attachment points on the airframe.
notes.explanation: On aircraft that have them, moveable control surfaces steer the aircraft, so both the surfaces and where they attach are checked.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 4, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to check about servo motors?
notes.back: The servos and their attachment points.
notes.explanation: A servo is a small motor that moves a control surface; its mounting is checked as well as the motor.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 5, p. 7-3

notes.front: Which parts of the propulsion system does the AC’s preflight list include?
notes.back: Powerplants, propellers, rotors, ducted fans and similar.
notes.explanation: The powerplant is the motor or engine, and a ducted fan is a propeller inside a ring-shaped duct: whatever drives the aircraft is checked.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 6, p. 7-3

notes.front: For a fuelled small UA, what does the AC’s preflight list say to check about fuel?
notes.back: The correct type and quantity.
notes.explanation: This applies only to fuel-powered aircraft; the list checks battery levels separately.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 7, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to check about equipment such as a camera?
notes.back: That it is securely attached.
notes.explanation: A camera or other payload that works loose can fall, or shift the aircraft’s balance in flight.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 8, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to check between aircraft and control station?
notes.back: That control link connectivity is established.
notes.explanation: Section 107.49 also requires the remote PIC to ensure all control links work before flight.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 9, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to verify about GPS?
notes.back: That GPS location is acquired from the manufacturer’s minimum number of satellites.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer sets the minimum number of satellites; the AC lists this check twice, once on its own and once with the communication check.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 10, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to verify about power for all systems?
notes.back: That aircraft and control unit have adequate power for the operation and work properly.
notes.explanation: Section 107.49(d) requires enough available power for the intended operational time.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 11, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to verify about avionics?
notes.back: Correct indications, including the control link transceiver, communication/navigation equipment and antennas.
notes.explanation: Avionics are the aircraft’s electronic systems; the transceiver is the radio that both sends and receives on the control link.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 12, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to check about a display panel, if used?
notes.back: That it is functioning properly.
notes.explanation: If a display panel is used, the remote PIC depends on it for flight information, so it must work before launch.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 13, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to check about ground support equipment?
notes.back: Its proper operation, including takeoff and landing systems.
notes.explanation: Equipment on the ground used for takeoff and landing is part of the system too, so it is checked with the aircraft.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 14, p. 7-3

notes.front: Besides link connectivity, what does the AC’s preflight list say to verify between control station and aircraft?
notes.back: That communication between them is adequate.
notes.explanation: Connectivity alone is not enough: communication must be adequate, and GPS lock is confirmed at the same time.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 15, p. 7-3

notes.front: How does the AC’s preflight list say to check control surface movement?
notes.back: By operating them from the control station and checking they move correctly.
notes.explanation: Operating the controls from the control station shows the whole chain, from input to surface, works.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 16, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say about a flight termination system?
notes.back: Check it, if the aircraft has one.
notes.explanation: A flight termination system deliberately ends a flight, e.g. by cutting power or deploying a parachute; if fitted, it must work.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 17, p. 7-3

notes.front: When does the AC’s preflight list require checking the anti-collision light?
notes.back: When operating in civil twilight or at night.
notes.explanation: Section 107.29 requires a light visible for at least 3 statute miles in civil twilight and at night.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 18, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to do with the compass?
notes.back: Calibrate it before any flight.
notes.explanation: The AC says to calibrate before any flight, not only after moving to a new site.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 19, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to verify about the controller?
notes.back: That it operates correctly for heading and altitude.
notes.explanation: It confirms that heading and altitude commands from the controller give the expected response.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 20, p. 7-3

notes.front: Why does the AC’s preflight list say to start the propellers before flight?
notes.back: To inspect for any imbalance or irregular operation.
notes.explanation: A damaged or imbalanced propeller shows up as irregular running on the ground, before it can fail in the air.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 21, p. 7-3

notes.front: What does the AC’s preflight list say to do at a controlled low altitude?
notes.back: Fly within range of any interference and recheck all controls and stability.
notes.explanation: A short, controlled flight low down and within range of any interference shows control or stability problems before the flight proper.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 22, p. 7-3

notes.front: Whose battery levels does the AC’s preflight list say to check?
notes.back: Both the aircraft’s and the control station’s.
notes.explanation: Both the aircraft and the control station need power for the whole flight (§ 107.49).
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 23, p. 7-3

notes.front: Why is part 43 appendix D not a complete small UAS inspection guide?
notes.back: It does not address UAS-specific features such as datalinks or support equipment.
notes.explanation: An operator using it must identify and add the items it does not cover.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.3, p. 7-2

notes.front: What makes part 43 appendix D a useful guide for building an inspection programme?
notes.back: It divides the aircraft into subgroups, giving a logical, systematic order.
notes.explanation: Airframe, then flight controls, then batteries, then engine, and so on.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.3, p. 7-2

notes.front: In what format may small UAS maintenance records be kept?
notes.back: A hardcopy and/or electronic logbook.
notes.explanation: The logbook covers periodic inspections, maintenance, preventive maintenance, repairs and alterations.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.5, p. 7-4

notes.front: Small UAS records should cover every component: the aircraft, the control station, launch and recovery equipment, the payload and the {{c1::command and control (C2) link equipment}}.
notes.explanation: Everything required to operate safely belongs in the records, not just the aircraft.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.5, p. 7-4

notes.front: What main benefit does recording repairs with time-in-service give?
notes.back: It lets the operator establish a reliable maintenance schedule for the small UAS and its components.
notes.explanation: It also tracks component service life and failure events.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.5, p. 7-4

notes.front: How do maintenance and inspection records support the decision to launch?
notes.back: They give retrievable evidence of the condition of safety-critical systems and components.
notes.explanation: For operators who fly many hours, records may be an essential safety support.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.5, p. 7-4

notes.front: Does AC 107-2A present record keeping for a non-Category 4 small UAS as mandatory or as beneficial?
notes.back: Beneficial: owners and operators “may find recordkeeping to be beneficial”.
notes.explanation: Category 4 aircraft have mandatory record rules under §107.140.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.5, p. 7-4

notes.front: Under AC 107-2A’s condition chart, what should you do if you notice structural or skin cracking?
notes.back: Inspect further for the scope of damage and hidden damage to structural integrity, then assess repairs.
notes.explanation: Table C-1 lists eleven conditions that may mean the small UA is not in a condition for safe operation.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 1, p. C-1

notes.front: Under AC 107-2A’s condition chart, what should you do if glued layers of the frame start to separate (delamination)?
notes.back: Inspect further for the scope of damage and hidden damage to structural integrity, then assess repairs.
notes.explanation: Table C-1 lists eleven conditions that may mean the small UA is not in a condition for safe operation.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 2, p. C-1

notes.front: Under AC 107-2A’s condition chart, what should you do if you notice a strong fuel smell?
notes.back: Find the source; leakage may be escaping or collecting in a sealed compartment, a fire risk.
notes.explanation: Table C-1 lists eleven conditions that may mean the small UA is not in a condition for safe operation.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 4, p. C-2

notes.front: Under AC 107-2A’s condition chart, what should you do if you notice a smell of electrical burning or arcing?
notes.back: Find the source of the possible electrical malfunction, which may pose a risk of fire or extreme heat.
notes.explanation: Table C-1 lists eleven conditions that may mean the small UA is not in a condition for safe operation.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 5, p. C-2

notes.front: Under AC 107-2A’s condition chart, what should you do if you notice black soot tracings or sparking?
notes.back: Treat as electrical burning or arcing: find the source of the possible electrical malfunction.
notes.explanation: Table C-1 lists eleven conditions that may mean the small UA is not in a condition for safe operation.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 6, p. C-2

notes.front: Under AC 107-2A’s condition chart, what should you do if you notice a noticeable change in propulsion sound during operation?
notes.back: Inspect the whole aircraft, especially motors and propellers, for damage or diminished performance.
notes.explanation: Table C-1 lists eleven conditions that may mean the small UA is not in a condition for safe operation.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 7, p. C-2

notes.front: What may a bulging battery casing indicate?
notes.back: Impending failure, with abrupt power loss and/or explosion.
notes.explanation: An electrical hazard may be present, with risk of fire or extreme heat.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 9, p. C-3

notes.front: If control inputs are delayed or out of sync, what action does Table C-1 give?
notes.back: Discontinue flight, or avoid further flight, until the control link has been inspected and tested.
notes.explanation: Reliable control communication must be restored first, to avoid loss of control or a flyaway.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 8, p. C-2

notes.front: What may diminishing flight time on an electric-powered small UA indicate?
notes.back: Impending battery failure, from exhausted service life or internal or external damage.
notes.explanation: Inspect the battery’s integrity as a reliable power source.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 10, p. C-3

notes.front: What risks do loose or missing fasteners pose?
notes.back: Changed flight characteristics, structural failure, dropped objects, loss of the aircraft, and danger to people and property.
notes.explanation: Secure loose hardware, and replace any that cannot be secured or is missing.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 11, p. C-3

notes.front: Why is liquid or gel leakage treated as an unsafe condition?
notes.back: It may pose a risk of fire, with extreme heat affecting structure, performance and flight duration.
notes.explanation: Find the source of the leak before further flight.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 3, p. C-1

notes.front: Before any flight in civil twilight or at night, what must the remote PIC confirm about the anti-collision light?
notes.back: That it functions properly.
notes.explanation: The AC’s preflight list includes this check.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.11.1 item 5, p. 5-10

notes.front: Why might a remote PIC shorten a planned night flight during preflight?
notes.back: The anti-collision light draws power, so the flight must leave enough to keep it lit and reach a normal landing.
notes.explanation: The remote PIC must consider whether the light reduces the power available.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.11.1 item 5, p. 5-10

notes.front: Does routine maintenance that does not change a Category 2 or 3 aircraft’s configuration or characteristics need a new declaration of compliance?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Example: replacing propellers, when the operating instructions list that as an allowed modification.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶8.4.5, p. 8-11

notes.front: When does replacing propellers on a Category 2 or 3 aircraft require a new declaration of compliance?
notes.back: When the replacement is not covered by the remote pilot operating instructions.
notes.explanation: Operating instructions should list allowed modifications so the aircraft stays eligible.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶8.4.5, p. 8-11

notes.front: At preflight you notice one battery’s case has swollen. What should you do?
notes.back: Do not fly it; inspect its integrity, as it may fail abruptly or explode.
notes.choices:
A) Fly it, but land with extra reserve
B) Keep it out of use and inspect it
C) Fly it only in daylight
notes.choicesExplained: A: a bulging battery may fail abruptly, so reserve does not make it safe. C: the risk of fire or power loss is the same by day.
notes.explanation: A distorted battery casing is on the AC’s list of unsafe conditions.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 9, p. C-3

notes.front: During a hover test, the aircraft responds to your stick inputs a moment late. What should you do?
notes.back: Stop flying until the control link has been inspected and tested and reliable control is restored.
notes.explanation: Delayed or unsynchronised inputs risk loss of control or a flyaway.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 8, p. C-2

notes.front: In flight, one motor starts to sound noticeably different. After landing, what should you inspect?
notes.back: The whole aircraft, with emphasis on motors and propellers, for damage or reduced performance.
notes.explanation: A noticeable sound change in the propulsion system is a listed unsafe condition.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 7, p. C-2

notes.front: After landing you smell burning electronics and see black soot marks near a motor lead. What kind of problem is this?
notes.back: A possible electrical malfunction, with risk of fire or extreme heat.
notes.explanation: Burning smells and soot tracings are both listed signs of electrical burning or arcing.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 items 5–6, p. C-2

notes.front: Your preflight finds a hairline crack in an arm. What does AC 107-2A tell you to do?
notes.back: Inspect further for the scope and any hidden damage, and assess repairs before flying.
notes.explanation: All required maintenance should be completed before each flight; flight operations should not occur until the issue is corrected.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶App. C, Table C-1 item 1, p. C-1; FAA Advisory Circular 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.2 and ¶7.2.3.1

notes.front: The manufacturer says to replace propellers every 50 flight hours; your log shows 50 hours. Is replacing them scheduled or unscheduled maintenance?
notes.back: Scheduled maintenance.
notes.explanation: It is driven by a time-in-service limit; unscheduled maintenance arises outside the schedule.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.1, p. 7-1

notes.front: The manufacturer pushes an urgent firmware update to fix a flight-control bug. What kind of maintenance is installing it?
notes.back: Unscheduled maintenance.
notes.explanation: A manufacturer may require an unscheduled software update to correct a problem.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.2, p. 7-1

notes.front: Your custom-built drone came with no maintenance schedule. How can you create one?
notes.back: Record every repair or replacement with the component’s time-in-service, and build a schedule from those records.
notes.explanation: Over time the data shows how long each component lasts.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.1.1, p. 7-1

notes.front: Your drone’s manufacturer says a gimbal repair must be done by its authorised service centre. Who should do it?
notes.back: The authorised service centre the manufacturer specifies.
notes.explanation: Some tasks must be done by the manufacturer or personnel it specifies.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.3, p. 7-1

notes.front: A technician tries but cannot restore a damaged motor to its safe operating specification. What next?
notes.back: You should replace the motor with one in a condition for safe operation.
notes.explanation: A component that cannot be returned to its safe specification should be replaced.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.3.1, p. 7-2

notes.front: You plan a 25-minute flight after sunset with a battery that lasts 27 minutes by day. What should your preflight consider?
notes.back: Check the anti-collision light works and whether its power draw means shortening the flight.
notes.explanation: There must be enough power to keep the light lit and still reach a normal landing.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.11.1 item 5, p. 5-10

notes.front: Your Category 2 drone’s operating instructions allow only the maker’s propellers. You fit cheaper third-party ones. Can you still fly Category 2 over people?
notes.back: No; that replacement is not covered by the instructions, so a new declaration of compliance would be needed.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, propellers are routine maintenance
B) No, a new declaration of compliance would be needed
C) Yes, if you log the change
notes.choicesExplained: A: routine propeller replacement keeps eligibility only when the instructions allow it. C: logging does not replace a declaration of compliance.
notes.explanation: Only modifications allowed by the remote pilot operating instructions keep the aircraft eligible.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶8.4.5, p. 8-11

notes.front: Before today’s flight, which navigation item on the AC’s preflight list do you do every time?
notes.back: Calibrate the compass (the AC recommends this before any flight).
notes.explanation: It sits alongside checking GPS lock from the manufacturer’s minimum satellites.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 19, p. 7-3

notes.front: After checking props visually, what functional check does the AC recommend to find a subtle propeller problem?
notes.back: Start the propellers and check for imbalance or irregular operation.
notes.explanation: Then, at low altitude, recheck controls and stability.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 21, p. 7-3

notes.front: During preflight you see the registration label has peeled half off. Which recommended preflight item has flagged a problem?
notes.back: The check that registration markings are properly displayed and legible.
notes.explanation: Marking must meet part 48; the AC includes it in the 23 preflight items.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 3, p. 7-3

notes.front: You own a Category 4 aircraft. A mechanic replaces a motor. What must the record show?
notes.back: A description of the work, the date completed, and the mechanic’s name.
notes.explanation: Category 4 maintenance records have content rules under §107.140(c).
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.140(c) “Category 4 operations” (maintenance requirements) (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A friend with no tools or training offers to repair your Category 4 aircraft. May he?
notes.back: No; the person must have the knowledge, skill and appropriate equipment for the work.
notes.explanation: Category 4 maintenance has regulatory requirements beyond the AC’s best practices.
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.140(c) “Category 4 operations” (maintenance requirements) (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: You fly 30 hours a week and keep no logbook. What does AC 107-2A suggest you are missing?
notes.back: A reliable maintenance schedule and evidence of component condition for the decision to launch.
notes.explanation: For operators accumulating hours fast, records may be an essential safety support.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.5, p. 7-4

notes.front: You build your inspection programme from part 43 appendix D. What must you add?
notes.back: Items it does not cover, such as datalinks and support equipment.
notes.explanation: Appendix D is a manned-aircraft checklist and is not comprehensive for UAS.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.3, p. 7-2

notes.front: Is installing a manufacturer firmware update part of maintaining your small UAS?
notes.back: Yes; system software upgrades are part of small UAS maintenance.
notes.explanation: The AC’s definition covers overhaul, repair, inspection, modification, replacement and software upgrades.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2, p. 7-1

notes.front: Your preflight covers the aircraft only. What does AC 107-2A say an appropriate preflight should encompass?
notes.back: The entire system, including the control station, links and support equipment, not just the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The inspection should be scalable to the aircraft, programme and operation.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.2, p. 7-2

notes.front: Scheduled versus unscheduled maintenance: which follows time-in-service limits?
notes.back: Scheduled; unscheduled maintenance arises outside the schedule, from use, a mishap or a required update.
notes.explanation: All required maintenance should be completed before each flight.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2.1–7.2.2, p. 7-1

notes.front: Maintenance versus preflight inspection: which must be done before every flight?
notes.back: The preflight inspection; maintenance is done when scheduled or when a problem is found.
notes.explanation: The preflight inspection is often where the need for unscheduled maintenance is discovered.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.2–7.3, p. 7-2

notes.front: Category 4 versus other small UAS: for which are maintenance records required by regulation?
notes.back: Category 4; for others AC 107-2A presents record keeping as a beneficial practice.
notes.explanation: Category 4 records must show the work, the date and who did it.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.5, p. 7-4
